verses.restored: Solomon built his own house thirteen years, and he finished all his house.
He built House of Forest of Lebanon: one hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high, upon four rows of cedar pillars with cedar beams upon pillars.
It was roofed with cedar above chambers upon forty-five pillars, fifteen in a row.
There were window frames in three rows, light opposite light in three ranks.
All entrances and doorposts were square with frames, and light was opposite light in three ranks.
He made Porch of Pillars, fifty cubits long and thirty wide, with a porch before them and pillars and threshold before them.
He made Porch of Throne where he judged, Porch of Judgment, covered with cedar from floor to floor.
His house where he lived had another court within porch, of similar work. Solomon also made a house like this porch for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken.
All these were costly stones, cut to measure, sawed with saws inside and outside, from foundation to coping and outside toward great court.
Foundation was costly, great stones—stones of ten cubits and stones of eight cubits.
Above were costly stones cut to measure and cedar.
Great court around had three rows of hewn stone and one row of cedar beams, as inner court of house of YHWH and porch of house.
King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre.

He was son of a widow from tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a Tyrian man, a bronze worker. He was filled with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge to do all work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work.
He cast two bronze pillars, each eighteen cubits high; a cord of twelve cubits surrounded each.
He made two capitals of cast bronze to set upon tops of pillars; height of each capital was five cubits.
Networks of latticework and wreaths of chainwork were for capitals atop pillars, seven for one and seven for other.
He made pillars with two rows of pomegranates around one network to cover capitals; thus for other capital.
Capitals atop pillars were of lily work in porch, four cubits.
Capitals upon two pillars had pomegranates above near belly beside network, two hundred in rows around each capital.
He raised pillars at porch of temple. He raised right pillar and named it Jachin; he raised left pillar and named it Boaz.
Upon tops of pillars was lily work. Work of pillars was finished.
He made a cast sea, ten cubits from brim to brim, round all around, five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits surrounded it.
Under its brim around were gourds, ten to a cubit, surrounding sea in two rows cast with it.
It stood upon twelve oxen: three facing north, three west, three south, and three east. Sea was above them, and all their backs turned inward.
It was a handbreadth thick; its brim was made like brim of cup, like lily blossom. It held two thousand baths.
He made ten bronze stands, each four cubits long, four wide, and three high.
Work of stands was this: they had panels, and panels were between frames.
Upon panels between frames were lions, oxen, and cherubim; above frames was a pedestal, and beneath lions and oxen were wreaths of hanging work.
Each stand had four bronze wheels and bronze axles. Its four feet had supports; beneath basin supports were cast beside each wreath.
Its opening within crown and above was one cubit; opening was round like pedestal, one and a half cubits, and upon opening were carvings. Panels were square, not round.
Four wheels were beneath panels, and wheel axles were in stand; height of each wheel was one and a half cubits.
Work of wheels was like chariot wheels; their axles, rims, spokes, and hubs were all cast.
Four supports were at four corners of each stand; supports were of stand itself.
On top of stand was round band half a cubit high; on top, supports and panels were of one piece with it.
Upon plates of supports and panels he engraved cherubim, lions, and palms, according to space of each, with wreaths around.
Thus he made ten stands; all had one casting, one measure, and one form.
He made ten bronze basins; each held forty baths and was four cubits; one basin upon each of ten stands.
He placed five stands on right side of house and five on left; sea he placed on right side of house, eastward toward south.
Hiram made basins, shovels, and bowls. Hiram finished doing all work he made for King Solomon for house of YHWH:
two pillars, bowls of capitals atop pillars, and two networks covering bowls of capitals;
four hundred pomegranates for two networks, two rows for each network covering bowls of capitals;
ten stands and ten basins upon stands;
one sea and twelve oxen beneath sea;
pots, shovels, and bowls. All these vessels Hiram made for King Solomon for house of YHWH were polished bronze.
In plain of Jordan king cast them in clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan.
Solomon left all vessels unweighed because they were exceedingly many; weight of bronze was not investigated.
Solomon made all vessels belonging to house of YHWH: gold altar and gold table upon which was bread of Presence;
lampstands of pure gold, five on right and five on left before inner sanctuary, with flowers, lamps, and tongs of gold;
cups, snuffers, bowls, spoons, firepans of pure gold, and gold hinges for doors of inner house, most holy place, and doors of temple house.
All work King Solomon made for house of YHWH was finished. Solomon brought things David his father had dedicated—silver, gold, and vessels—and placed them among treasures of house of YHWH.

translation_notes: Solomon spends thirteen years on his palace complex after seven years on the temple. The juxtaposition invites scrutiny of royal self-investment beside sacred devotion.
Pharaoh's daughter receives a palace but remains unnamed and represented through Solomon's marriage acquisition.
Hiram the artisan—not Hiram the king—is a widow's son with Israelite and Tyrian family ties. His craft wisdom is central and should not disappear under Solomon's authorship.
The bronze work celebrates technical knowledge, casting, measurement, engineering, and art. Skilled manual labor is wisdom.
Pillars, pomegranates, lilies, palms, lions, oxen, cherubim, and the sea create a symbolic cosmos of stability, fertility, royal force, and sacred presence.
The twelve bronze oxen are crafted supports, but animal imagery should not erase the living animals consumed throughout the cultic system.
The unweighed abundance of bronze and extensive gold point to enormous extraction, transport, furnace labor, fuel use, and wealth concentration.
David and Solomon receive narrative credit, while Hiram and countless miners, charcoal makers, mold builders, carriers, polishers, and assistants remain mostly unnamed.
safety_note: Do not use sacred or royal beauty to erase labor, ecology, wealth concentration, gendered dynastic arrangements, or foreign expertise. Artisanship is wisdom, and workers are not extensions of a king's glory.
